articles.title: The KP impasse
articles.content: SUNDAY brought what was being whispered about in Islamabad for days: the dismissal of the PTI government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The whispers hadturned into newsby Saturday. All day long, the mainstream media kept reporting on the possibility of an emergency, adding that the prime minister would hold a cabinet meeting on Sunday morning to make the ‘final’ decision. But by Saturday evening, there were many other meetings as politicians from the government and opposition sides met or held consultations publicly and behind the scenes. These were last-ditch efforts to avoid taking a ‘painful decision’. There was little clarity on what the outcome of these comings and goings would be. Apart from the government and PTI, the JUI-F, too, had jumped into the fray and offered to mediate between the two sides. In fact, on Sunday morning, channelsreportedthat the prime minister called Maulana Fazlur Rahman during the meeting, creating the impression that some last-minute deal was being thrashed out. But clearly, these were red herrings, for soon it was announced that both an emergency and governors’ rule had been imposed. It later transpired that the call was simply to inform the maulana about the decision. The cabinet meeting was followed by a bunch of ministers, including of law and interior, holding a press conference to justify their decision. They all looked a bit glum; perhaps they hadn’t slept much. The PTI’s reaction was muted as it was limited to social media. It seemed as if the television channels were not covering what was happening in KP; neither did they report on the fate of the PTI leadership. Social media posts claimed that the chief minister, Sohail Afridi, as well as other officials, including the KP Assembly Speaker, had been picked up. However, the number of those picked up or arrested is not known; there is little reporting on the issue and the government isn’t willing to provide details. It seems the party’s coverage on the mainstream electronic media is being limited. By the evening, anadvisory councilhad been put together, in which individuals were given portfolios. It also held a meet-and-greet session with the governor. From the details provided about the people and their portfolios, it seems that far more time had gone into the decision than a mere 24 hours. This is something that was lent more credence by the press conference by Maulana Fazlur Rahman, who alleged that the government had backed out of talks. Governance by a technocratic administration in KP will help the PTI retain its popularity. Interestingly, the federal government has imposed an emergency as well as governor’s rule. The logic is hard to understand, though one lawyer suggested it may be because governor’s rule has a time limit while an emergency endorsed by parliament doesn’t. The federal government didn’t want a time limit or to leave the PTI government in place; hence, it used both. And with the kind of administrative measures taken, along with the cabinet announced, it doesn’t seem the new set-up is here for a short time. In the coming days, there will be much hand-wringing over the role of the PPP and the PML-N in dismissing a democratically elected government. But perhaps this is the price they had to pay to keep enjoying power without mandate. The two parties had got off the democracy train some time ago. At the moment, there is little likelihood of them getting back on. But this is not to say they can’t clamber back on; after all the party that has opposed Sunday’s decision unequivocally is the JUI-F, which was once part and parcel of a set-up introduced by Gen Musharraf. In the land of the pure, parties find new positions quickly. They discover democracy again and again and again. It is a bit like some of us enjoy returning to the same books again and again; the familiarity is what makes it comforting. However, what will not be easily forgotten is this notion of political parties based in Sindh and Punjab adding to the instability facing the other half of Pakistan — Balochistan and KP, which face the brunt of the violence. Now on to the issue of terrorism, which allegedly led to the decision to dismiss the KP government. Terrorism’s reincarnation in KP is a complex subject. It cannot be tackled in an article on politics but suffice it to say that this new set-up will not have much impact on the violence in the province. This is partly because terrorism was provided as a justification for the decision to impose an emergency, and is not the reason behind the dismissal of the PTI government, and partly because the government’s argument contradicts itself — it blames the PTI for not providing the political ownership of the state’s effort against terrorism and then proceeds to replace an elected government with a technocratic set-up. How will this provide the much-needed ownership? More serious still is the decision of the federal government and establishment to take over the province and directly assume responsibility for all that happens there. If in the coming weeks and months, terrorism does not subside, there will be no PTI to blame. The failure — if it is there — will be Islamabad’s and Pindi’s to own. The failure will not be one related to terrorism solely, but will also include governance matters, and the economic hardship faced across the country. These are all issues the lengthy caretaker government in KP faced and apparently failed to resolve. For this is why a populace tiring of the PTI voted back the party with a two-thirds majority in the provincial assembly. And since 2024, the shenanigans of Ali Amin Gandapur and Sohail Afridi once again led to disenchantment among the KP voters. However, governance by a technocratic administration will once again help the PTI retain its popularity, even though its second-tier leadership will face hardship, including arrests or kidnapping. But once these subside, the party might just flex its muscles to return to power. Indeed, the weekend’s developments have brought no resolution to the political crisis in KP. The merry-go-round continues.
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: A juncture and a moment
articles.content: A CLUTCH of unforeseen events have combined to pose the existential crisis Prime Minister Narendra Modi is facing from unemployed youth and young students, who after claiming his education minister’s scalp recently are now determined to win the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, India’s chief election commissioner whom they call “a vote thief”. The first trigger for the youth to take to the streets came with the cancellation and corruption in the entrance exams to India’s medical colleges, which led to nationwide protests amid a dozen suicides by dejected students. Then the chief justice of India described unemployed youth as cockroaches, setting off a response nobody expected. But the safety pin from the fraught grenade was pulled by Ritika Chopra, who broke theIndian Expressstory on Sept 23 about two election commissioners officially calling out their chief Gyanesh Kumar for alleged illegalities in deleting 130 million voters from the electoral rolls. The deletions altered the outcomes in Bihar and West Bengal polls to the BJP’s advantage. That Modi is not prepared to allow the fall of a key pivot of his winning electoral machinery is evident from the paramilitary units he has mobilised, including from troubled Jammu and Kashmir and from platoons purposed to guard the frontier with Pakistan. They have been joined by the Delhi Police supported by street criminals from the Hindutva fold to jointly barricade New Delhi against protesters led largely by the recently formed Cockroach Janta Party. On their part, the Cockroaches are predominantly from the Hindu middle classes, which makes it a tricky proposition for Modi to use the lethal force he deployed against the Shaheen Bagh anti-citizenship laws campaign in 2020. That movement, led chiefly by swathes of brave Muslim women in Delhi, was broken by a combination of the Covid-19 pandemic and brute force that coincided with President Donald Trump’s visit to Gujarat. Trump lost the election and Joe Biden won it, only for Trump to stage a comeback, while two Muslim student activists, Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, picked up in the crackdown during his India visit six years ago, have marked time in prison. The Cockroach movement has gained credibility by underscoring its key objectives that Indians have been dreaming of. Last week, Khalid, detained without trial under draconian anti-terror laws, won the 2026 Award for Human Rights Defenders at Risk for the Asia and Pacific region, presented by the Ireland-based Front Line Defenders. It’s difficult to see the crass brutality of a combined force of Delhi Police and Hindutva squads visiting the current crop of protesters, even though they have attacked young women in particular several times. The protests have created an extremely critical moment for the Modi establishment and for the opposition, represented prominently by the feisty young woman leader Neha Bora from the left flank of national politics. The wide political support has added heft to the collective battle for Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. There has been some quibbling in the opposition ranks, principally between the Aam Aadmi Party and the Congress, about who is more committed to the students’ cause, but this has more to do with the political chance both are eyeing in Punjab, where they face each other in elections early next year. To be fair, the campaign against ‘vote theft’ began as Rahul Gandhi’s battle in mid-2023, when two laws were enacted that would be considered scandalous and unacceptable in any functioning democracy. Modi changed the mechanism that chose the poll chief. He replaced the chief justice of India from the troika that chose the poll chief with his cabinet minister, making the opposition’s presence meaningless. He also gave his handpicked election chief lifelong immunity from legal challenges for his duty in holding elections. The move paid off, with the poll body ignoring Modi’s communally polarising campaign and money power in the 2024 elections, without which he would perhaps have not got the 240 seats that were still 32 short of a majority. The Cockroach movement has gained credibility by underscoring its key objectives that Indians have been dreaming of. No chief justice shall be granted a Rajya Sabha seat as a post-retirement reward, it declared, the reference being to the reward going to the chief justice who gave the controversial Ayodhya judgement. The Cockroach agenda offered a dire warning to the poll chief. “If any legitimate vote is deleted, the chief election commissioner shall be arrested under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, as taking away voting rights is ‘no less than terrorism’.” The Cockroaches are committed to women getting 50 per cent reservation (instead of the 33pc promised at present) without increasing the strength of parliament. They want 50pc of all cabinet positions to be reserved for women by law. TV channels seen as loyal to Modi should be disbanded. “All media houses owned by the Gautam Adani Group and Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries shall have their licences cancelled to make way for independent media. Bank accounts of ‘Godi media anchors’ shall be investigated.” To political parties like the Congress, which has suffered a slew of defections to the BJP, the Cockroaches have offered relief. “Any member of the legislative assembly (MLA) or member of parliament (MP) who defects from one party to another shall be barred from contesting elections and holding public office for 20 years.” On its part, the Cockroaches promised to remain answerable under the RTI Act and refuse to accept any anonymous donations. It’s a given that much of the Cockroach agenda gestated in years of Rahul Gandhi’s critical campaigns. But is it helpful to squabble with each other when the idea is to seize the moment at this fraught juncture for Indian democracy? Mistrusting each other ended disastrously in Bihar and West Bengal for the INDIA group. Rahul sees Modi and key aides facing the law soon. To pursue the wish, he could trust the newly minted youth power and less so his party. The ‘party’ has been the bane of the Congress since Nehru’s time. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: Politics or ‘war’?
articles.content: OCTOBER has been most cruel to our fragile democracy. It has seen Liaquat Ali’s unresolved murder, 1954’s emergency, 1955’s One Unit move, Suhrawardy’s 1957 ouster, the 1958 and 1999 coups, governor’s rule in Sindh, and emergency/governor’s rule in KP now. This grim record reveals a deep malaise: broken institutions unable to resolve conflicts via reason and compromise, letting coercion fill the void. But no civilian era may have seen them as broken, biased and besmirched as now. A parliament born with a murky mandate has grown up to author partisan laws and fuel conflicts. Courts are seen as partisan players, not reliable referees. The executive uses one gear against dissent — force —true to its hybrid DNA. The contrast could not have been starker as the centre’s maximal rigidity faced the PTI’s minimal demands. The centre’s misrule and disputed mandate justify peaceful protests on much bigger demands across South Asia recently: freshpolls, free courts, human rights, and the economy. But the PTI only sought the mild relief that the courts had given their leader Imran Khan on meetings and medical care. The centre reacted to even these timid asks with threats of emergency rule which has now been imposed. It wanted the PTI to back a harsh Afghan eviction policy. But evicting Afghans in need of refuge from the Afghan Taliban’s sins is hardly fair. Some may qualify for nationality and many contribute capital and labour, replacing millions of us now abroad. We must, instead, sympathise with ordinary Afghans as both of us are the worst victims of the sins of the Taliban regime in Afghanistan. Mistreating them may boost our common foe. At the moment, ordinary Afghans here, far away from TTP training camps abroad, seem unlikely recruits. But harsh evictions may change both access and motive for some. The centre blames PTI for the failure to end KP terrorism. But the centre also notes that terrorists cross borders, thus indicating that the primary responsibility lies with itself. Inland too, federal forces flex bigger muscles than the KP Police. So, the responsibility must be shared. Also, any large operation may again displace locals and most KP parties oppose it. Intelligence-led commando action closely coordinated with locals seems more suitable both tactically and morally. Islamabad should have accepted these ground realities. The twin actions in KP will not help the centre. Given the minimalist demands and these policy nuances, the twin KP actions in the midst of talks and a slow-motion march seem harsh. There are many PTI faults but also reasons for them being rooted in the party’s repression since 2023. The centre has bigger faults and fewer excuses. It should have first fixed its own shortcomings to convince the PTI to fix its faults and then forged a joint anti-terrorism strategy. Instead, it seems bent on a winner-takes-all war, not win-win politics with rivals. Force has replaced laws, norms, reason, compromise and decency as its default tool. This aspect has taken many past conflicts from institutions to the streets, where the state prevails easily, and then to the bush, where it struggles to end even those that lack popular and moral roots. The twin actions in KP will not help the centre in either politics or security. Emergency rule may hand it administrative control in KP but not political authority. It may have tamed a hostile set-up but has also inflamed its voters. The vast power this regime has amassed has not translated into delivery, and is even less unlikely to do so in a troubled KP with an ad hoc, unpopular set-up. So, the PTI may gain politically as intensified repression helps it develop a victimhood narrative. Defeating terrorism needs both public support and arsenal. Emergency and governor’s rule in KP may erode support to levels no arsenal can compensate for. The key drivers of terrorism may persist too. TTP camps may survive cross-border bombing. Porous borders will persist despite harsh travel and trade bans if federal policing remains weak. The humility in a hybrid centre to adopt a terrorism policy that combines force with local wisdom and support may remain absent. It will gain an obedient KP junior partner, but one with weak support, legitimacy, and capacity. It has had such partners for decades in Balochistan, and yet terrorism persists there. KP may meet the same fate. The centre’s obsession with force may feed terrorism more than fight it. The writer has a PhD degree from the University of California, Berkeley, in political economy and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.
articles.author: Dr Niaz Murtaza

articles.title: Busting the myths
articles.content: INTELLECTUAL and wealthy Baloch are often a surprise for people in other parts of Pakistan. All preconceived notions stem from the stereotypical portrayals of the people of this vast province. As a result, the education, etiquette, intellect, and values of tolerance of the people of Balochistan are taken lightly. A classmate of mine was, as I recall, introduced at one of Pakistan’s elite universities, with particular emphasis not on her qualifications but on the remote area in Balochistan to which she belonged. She felt that she had been singled out. Another aspect is grouping Balochistan’s applicants for jobs with under-represented categories, which shows a general reluctance to mainstream them. Special concessions — including a higher age limit — introduced to expand job opportunities in Balochistan also reinforce a sense of marginalisation. For example, when someone who holds an MPhil degree is accepted in a position that requires a PhD degree, it implies that candidates from Balochistan are not expected to compete on an equal footing with the others. All this is due to the lack of knowledge about the geography, history, heritage, cultural and linguistic diversity of this land. Balochistan has valuable natural resources as well as the values of love, tolerance, openness, coexistence, and acumen. But, its cultural wealth has not been understood. Moreover, around seven different languages are spoken across the province. These represent seven distinct identities, each with its own cultural norms, values, and legacy. This diverse linguistic landscape is a true example of coexistence. Despite deprivation, harsh sociopolitical conditions, a frail infrastructure, and serious security concerns, the Baloch people remain remarkably open-minded, intellectually charged, and socially aware. Indeed, their outlook and knowledge can match, and even surpass, that of people in the more developed parts of the country. Misconceptions have more to do with the lack of information about them. An analysis of formal education — educational institutions and curricula — and public awareness platforms, such as media and political discourse, often do not do justice to this region. Syllabi and textbooks also fail to inform the public. A more inclusive and balanced understanding of the province’s strengths and challenges must become a part of formal education, including through curricula and textbooks, educational policies and plans, and educational governance systems. A deeper, more nuanced understanding of the Baloch is essential. However, Balochistan should not be represented in the curriculum through the lens of deprivation. Prospectuses should integrate local languages, histories, literature, oral traditions, indigenous knowledge, and contemporary achievements alongside high-quality scientific and professional education — enabling students to view their heritage not as a marker of marginality but as a source of knowledge, identity, and possibility. Academic policies need to also be framed around the intellectual, cultural, and human resources within the province. The media must not sensationalise the province’s sense of deprivation, reduce its people to tales of backwardness, or exploit their grievances for political or commercial purposes. Instead, it should present an accurate, nuanced image of Balochistan, extensively cover the issues its people face, and remain attentive to the province’s historical, social, and political context. In this way, the media can contribute to a more informed national understanding, which is always more beneficial than reinforcing stereotypes and deepening grievances. The political elite must not view marginalisation as a politically viable resource, or allow dependency and criticism to persist in order to consolidate its authority. Instead, they need to remain connected and work collectively to address the underlying challenges of the province. Meaningful political engagement requires accessibility and inclusion. Many political events, such as all-party conferences, are held in the federal capital, making them financially inaccessible to representatives of side-lined communities, and thereby limiting their participation in the national political discourse. Ultimately, positive narratives are essential not only to address deprivation but also to reveal the true wealth of Balochistan, ie, its people, who are as capable, valuable, and deserving of recognition as any other citizen elsewhere in the country. Above all, such efforts can help overcome the persistent ‘curse’ which obscures their real identity, tolerance, capacity for coexistence, and intellectual potential. This vast and ancient land has to be celebrated for the strength and inclusive values of its people.
articles.author: Nazir A. Jogezai

articles.title: Yemen escalation
articles.content: WITH the Houthi Ansarallah movement continuing to target Saudi Arabia, the region stands at a perilous juncture. The Houthi attacks — particularly those targeting the airport at Riyadh — are becoming increasingly destructive, with several peoplekilledand hundreds reportedly injured in Saturday’s strike. The attack was said to be the deadliest the kingdom has witnessed in years. The airport attacks have been condemned internationally, and there have been mass flight cancellations. The Saudis, who are backing the anti-Houthi Yemeni government, are poised to strike back at the pro-Iran group with even greater force. Yet a small window of opportunity has opened up, with the Iranian and Saudi foreign ministers discussing matters over the phone on Sunday. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reportedly told his Saudi counterpart Faisal bin Farhan that a military approach would “complicate” matters in Yemen, while offering Tehran’s good offices to mediate with Ansarallah. The Houthis are independent actors; framing them as the puppets of Tehran is inaccurate. Yet they do share ideological and geopolitical ground with Iran, and if Tehran talks, the Houthis are bound to listen. Therefore, involving Iran in talks between the Saudis and Houthis could produce positive results. If Riyadh has any reservations, Pakistan — which maintains channels with both Saudi Arabia and Iran — could also be involved. Oman could be another mediating party, as the sultanate has close ties with both Riyadh and Tehran, besides maintaining an open line with the Houthis. The fact is that Muslim countries — Arab and non-Arab — have a significant role to play in defusing the situation both within Yemen and between Saudi Arabia and Ansarallah. The US has threatened to get involved in Yemen militarily again. This would be a recipe for great disaster. America has done enough damage in the Middle East, and it is the regional states that must lead the peace process. Whether Iran’s offer is accepted, or Pakistan and Oman attempt a fresh push for a negotiated settlement, some key points must be kept in mind if there is to be long-term peace. Firstly, the mutual security of Saudi Arabia and Yemen must be prioritised, and the targeting of civilian targets, such as airports, must stop. A temporary truce should then be called to allow the two sides a cooling-off period and come to the negotiating table. Within Yemen, durable peace can only be achieved through a Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned process, which takes on board all the country’s tribes and communities. Such an agreement can also help bring peace to Saudi Arabia, while ending Yemen’s humanitarian nightmare. However, escalation from either side can turn the Yemeni conflict into a regional war — something that all peace brokers must do their utmost to prevent.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Inequitable taxation
articles.content: FINANCE Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb has once more reviewed the latest incentive scheme to bring retailers into the tax net — and again, the meeting last week took place against disappointing results. Mr Aurangzeb says that the retailers’ tax scheme should not be seen as a one-year arrangement. That is an admission in itself. A simplified route, offered on easy terms, has not persuaded the sector to join, and the government is now preparing for a long wait. This is not the first attempt. Tajir Dost drew only about 58,000 registrations, according to reports, and was said to be falling short of its revenue target of Rs50bn. Before it came fixed-tax regimes, amnesties and reduced rates. Each ended with a new scheme being drawn up. Clearly, traders and wholesalers will not enter the system voluntarily, when staying out costs nothing. Incentives work when the alternative is a penalty. Instead, retail, real estate, and agriculture are the three major sectors the state has never taxed in proportion to their size. Retail has shutter-down power: the threat of a strike that closes markets has made governments retreat from documentation attempts. The numbers show who pays. In FY26, the salaried class paid Rs633bn in income tax, far more than real estate and retailers put together. Salaried people are taxed at source and cannot hide; a retailer dealing in cash can. The organised corporate sector, which carries the super tax and high advance taxes, is in the same position. The burden falls on the documented, because they are the easiest to reach. A narrow base keeps rates high for those inside it, discouraging formal employment and investment. It starves the budget of money for social spending, so the gap is filled by borrowing and squeezing health, education, and infrastructure. Slower growth, fewer jobs, and more poverty follow; these, in turn, shrink the base. The government cannot keep financing itself in this manner. The way out is not another scheme. Instead, retailers and wholesalers should be treated like other taxpayers. That means compulsory registration, integration of point-of-sale systems with the FBR, and the use of electricity connections, bank transactions, and rent and property data to identify the unregistered. A tax system that exempts the powerful and burdens the compliant cannot support growth and cannot be defended as fair. Every kind of income must be taxed equitably.
articles.author: Editorial
